newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's QSC says hedging sugar prices.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's QSC says hedging sugar prices.

text.p: The Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC) said had secured higher sugar prices for future years through a medium-term hedging programme which was expected to benefit the Australian industry by A$30 million over three years.

Increasing world sugar production and decreasing availability of long-term contracts had significantly increased exposure to the vagaries of world markets, it said in its annual report for the year ended June 30.
Despite a world sugar surplus of about five million tonnes, prices held up remarkably well in 1995/96 even though they were lower than the year before, it said.
This was largely because much of the surplus stock was contained within India and the European Union (EU) and unavailable to be traded on the world market, it said.

With Queensland sugar sales primarily denominated in U.S. dollars, a one cent increase in the Australian dollar potentially decreased annual returns to the Queensland industry by A$15-A$20 million, it said.
In 1995/96 the Australian dollar rose to a high of US$0.8050 in May 1996 from $0.7292 in June 1995 before ending at $0.7878 in June 1996, it said.
Through risk management instruments QSC achieved an average Australian dollar/US dollar rate of $0.7387 for the year, it said.
Discussing financial risk prospects, QSC said analysts were forecasting similar world sugar production levels for this year to 1995/96 and an increase in world sugar consumption.
Brazil, Thailand and India, with record crops in 1995/96, had contributed to high stock levels, it said.
"With expansion set to continue in Thailand and Brazil in 1996/97, a significant improvement in price appears unlikely," it said.
"The anticipated higher world sugar consumption is not expected to offset production and a further addition to world stocks is forecast," it said.

The Australian dollar was expected to appreciate further in an environment of stronger world growth and commodity prices, improved economic fundamentals and continued offshore demand for the currency, QSC said.
